blocks.text: I can compare the characteristics of living things and describe their similarities and differences.
Tap each word to see what it means.

items.def: Something observable is something that we can see or describe using our senses.
A characteristic is a feature or quality of something that we can use to help identify it.
We compare things by looking at what is the same and what is different.
A similarity is something two or more objects have in common.
A difference between two objects or things is something that is not similar or the same about them.

blocks.text: Sofia wants to practise putting things into groups, using her friends. What could she use to divide them up?
These are all {observable characteristics}.
An observable characteristic is a feature or property of a living thing that we can see or use our other senses to observe. It can be about **colour**, **size**, **shape** or **structure**.
Some observable characteristics of Alex’s mum are that she has ginger hair, straight hair, blue eyes and freckles.
Some observable characteristics of Alex’s older sister are that she has ginger hair, curly hair, green eyes and freckles.

blocks.label: What do you notice?
blocks.text: You can compare them. They are **similar** because both have ginger hair and freckles. They are **different** because one has straight hair and blue eyes and the other has curly hair and green eyes.

blocks.q: Can we observe it? Put each one in the right column.

blocks.text: Sofia sorted herself and her friends into groups using an observable characteristic: children with curly hair and children with straight hair.
Alex had been put in the wrong group. He has curly hair, so he belongs in the curly hair group.
When sorting things into groups, the groups do not need to be equal in size.

blocks.q: When you sort things into groups, can one group have more things in it than another?
options: No, the groups must be the same size
Yes, the groups do not need to be equal in size
blocks.why: When sorting things into groups, the groups do not need to be equal in size.

blocks.text: When we compare things, we look at their similarities and differences.
Scientists use observable characteristics to compare living things. This helps them to sort living things into groups and work out what they are.
Sam compared a holly bush with a bramble. Both have green leaves and berries.

blocks.label: What are the differences?
blocks.text: The berries are different colours and shapes. The holly has spiky, waxy leaves and the bramble doesn’t.
Look at the tulips and buttercups in the lesson’s pictures. Aisha says their flowers are different. Izzy says their flowers are similar. Both children are correct!

items.title: Similar
items.sub: Both sit at the top of long, green stems and both have yellow petals.

items.title: Different
items.sub: The flowers have differences in their shapes and sizes.

blocks.text: Think about Alex’s mum (ginger hair, straight hair, blue eyes, freckles) and Alex’s older sister (ginger hair, curly hair, green eyes, freckles).

blocks.q: Is each characteristic a similarity or a difference between them?

items.text: one has straight hair, one has curly hair
one has blue eyes, one has green eyes

blocks.text: Which is the odd one out: a penguin, a butterfly or a macaw? Think about what is the same and what is different about each one.

blocks.label: Two ideas
blocks.text: The butterfly is the only one that is not a bird. The penguin can’t fly.

blocks.q: Which of these is an observable characteristic we could use to compare animals?
blocks.why: We can see or describe a body covering (such as fur or feathers). The date an animal was born is not an observable characteristic.

blocks.text: Lucas compared a fly, a blue tit and a tiger. He chose these observable characteristics to compare.

items: Colour: the fly is green, the blue tit is blue, black, yellow and white, the tiger is black, white and orange.
How it moves: the fly walks and flies, the blue tit walks and flies, the tiger walks, runs and climbs.
Number of legs: fly 6, blue tit 2, tiger 4.

blocks.q: In Lucas’s table, match each animal to its body covering.

blocks.text: Scientists can compare similarities and differences between living things to help work out whether they belong in certain groups.
Alex found an animal in his backyard. It has six legs and a pair of antennae, so he thinks it must be an insect. He compares it with bees, butterflies and moths.

blocks.label: What did he decide?
blocks.text: The shape of his insect’s body and wings is most similar to the moths, so he thinks it must be a type of moth. Now he can research using secondary sources to identify which type of moth it is.
Laura compared a bird in her garden with pigeons, finches and wagtails. She looked for the group it had most observable characteristics in common with.

blocks.label: Her reasoning
blocks.text: It is a type of finch. It has a similar body shape, a very similarly shaped beak and a short tail made of feathers like the finches. Pigeons have longer necks, and wagtails have a longer tail and beak.

blocks.q: How can we decide which group an unknown animal belongs to?
options: Pick the group it has the fewest things in common with
Pick the group it has the most observable characteristics in common with
Pick the group with the most animals
blocks.why: Alex and Laura both chose the group their animal had most in common with.

items: Observable characteristics are properties about things that we can describe using our five senses.
Living things have many observable characteristics we can use to compare similarities and differences between them.
Comparing and grouping living things can help us to identify them.

flashcards.back: Something we can see or describe using our senses.
A feature or quality of something that we can use to help identify it.

flashcards.front: What do we do when we compare things?
flashcards.back: We look at what is the same and what is different.
Something two or more objects have in common.
Something that is not similar or the same about two objects or things.

flashcards.front: Colour, size, shape and structure are examples of which kind of characteristics?
Give an example of something that is NOT an observable characteristic of an animal.
When sorting things into groups, do the groups need to be equal in size?
flashcards.back: No. The groups do not need to be equal in size.

flashcards.front: Why do scientists use observable characteristics to compare living things?
flashcards.back: It helps them sort living things into groups and work out what they are.

flashcards.front: Alex’s animal has six legs and a pair of antennae. What does he think it is?
How did Alex decide which group of insects his animal belonged to?
flashcards.back: He looked for the group it was most similar to. The shape of its body and wings was most similar to the moths.

flashcards.front: How did Laura decide which group her garden bird belonged to?
flashcards.back: She chose the group it had most observable characteristics in common with. It was a finch.

worksheet.title: Worksheet: Comparing characteristics of living things
worksheet.instructions: Answer each question with a word, a number or a short phrase, using what you learned in the lesson.

questions.prompt: What word means “something two or more objects have in common”?
questions.explanation: A similarity is something two or more objects have in common.

questions.prompt: What word means “something that is not similar or the same about two things”?
questions.explanation: A difference is something that is not similar or the same about two objects or things.

questions.prompt: What word means “a feature or quality of something that we can use to help identify it”?
questions.explanation: A characteristic is a feature or quality of something that we can use to help identify it.

questions.prompt: We compare things by looking at what is the same and what is ____.
questions.explanation: Comparing means looking at what is the same and what is different.

questions.prompt: Scientists use observable characteristics to compare living things. This helps them sort living things into ____.
questions.explanation: Comparing helps scientists sort living things into groups and work out what they are.

questions.prompt: In Lucas’s comparison table, how many legs does the blue tit have?
questions.explanation: Lucas’s table showed a fly with 6 legs, a blue tit with 2 legs and a tiger with 4 legs.

questions.prompt: In Lucas’s comparison table, what covers the body of the blue tit?
questions.explanation: The blue tit has feathers. The fly has very short hairs and the tiger has fur.

questions.prompt: A holly bush and a bramble were compared. Which one has spiky, waxy leaves?
questions.explanation: The holly has spiky, waxy leaves and the bramble doesn’t.

questions.prompt: Alex’s animal has six legs and a pair of antennae. Which group of animals does he think it must belong to?
questions.explanation: Alex looked at its observable characteristics: six legs and a pair of antennae. So he thinks it must be an insect.

questions.prompt: Alex compared his insect with bees, butterflies and moths. Which group was its body and wing shape most similar to?
questions.explanation: The shape of its body and wings was most similar to the moths.

questions.prompt: Laura compared her garden bird with pigeons, finches and wagtails. Which group did she decide it belonged to?
questions.explanation: It had a similar body shape, beak and short tail made of feathers, like the finches.
